say.text: An adult has burns over the whole head and neck, the whole front of the trunk, and the perineum.
Estimate the total body surface area (TBSA) with the adult rule of nines. What do you get?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Go region by region and give each one its own adult figure. Count the small perineum separately, not with the trunk.
That choice is not right. You have given the perineum a 9, the head's figure. Nines are the first figures most people memorise, so they stick to any small patch.
In the adult chart the perineum is 1% and the head and neck is 9%. Count each region at its own figure, then add them up.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one matters: the perineum is a small region, not a head-sized one.

say.text: That choice is not right. You have given the head and neck 18%, a trunk or leg figure. The big trunk numbers spill onto the head sitting beside them.
In the adult chart the head and neck is 9%, the same as each arm. Count it at 9% and add the regions again.

sure_note.text: You were sure about the head. Check that figure first next time: head and neck is 9%.

say.text: Yes. Head and neck 9, anterior trunk 18 and perineum 1 make 28%.
The adult rule of nines, in per cent: head and neck 9, each arm 9, front and back of the trunk 18 each, each leg 18, perineum 1.
Add the chart and it totals 100%. Count each region at its own figure, not the one you remember next to it.
A 2-year-old has scalds over the whole head and both legs.
Which method should you use to estimate the TBSA?

choices.label: Wallace rule of nines, adult values
Lund and Browder chart, scaled by age
Rule of nines, legs counted at 18% each
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Picture a toddler's body. Its head is proportionally bigger and its legs smaller than an adult's. Which chart accounts for that?
That choice is not right. You have reached for the adult chart, the one most people learn first. A scald looks like any other burn, so the familiar chart feels safe.
In a child the head is about 18% and each leg about 14%. The adult figures overstate the legs and understate the head, so age comes first.

sure_note.text: You were sure the adult chart fits any burn. It does not: age changes the proportions first.

say.text: That choice is not right. You have given each leg the adult 18%. Legs look large on any patient, so an adult leg figure feels safe.
In a toddler each leg is about 14%, so 18% overstates it. Age changes the figures for every region, not just the head.

sure_note.text: You were sure the leg was 18%. In a child it is nearer 14% each, so check the age first.

say.text: Yes. Lund and Browder corrects each region for age, so it suits a toddler's proportions.
Lund and Browder corrects the regional figures for age. In a child the head is about 18% and each leg about 14%.
Score every region on the age-based chart, not only the head and legs.
An infant has burns over the whole head and one whole leg.
Estimate the TBSA.

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Score the head and the leg each with the child figure, not the adult one. Then add the two.
That choice is not right. You have used the adult figures for both the head and the leg. Nines and eighteens feel like the default, so they come first.
An infant's head is about 18% and each leg about 14%. The adult head figure undercounts the head by half.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the age before the chart: an infant's head is about 18%.

say.text: That choice is not right. You have switched the head to the child figure but kept the leg at the adult 18%. Once one region looks right, the other feels right too.
An infant's leg is about 14%, the same age rule that gives the head 18%. Use one age rule for every region.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look at the leg too: an infant's leg is about 14%.

say.text: Yes. An infant's head is about 18% and each leg about 14%, so the head plus one leg makes 32%.
The figure is 32%: infant head 18% plus one leg 14%.
Child figures apply to every region of a toddler's body, so one age rule covers the whole chart.
The full adult rule of nines totals 100%.
Which figure belongs to the perineum?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Work out the big regions first, then ask which small figure completes the 100%.
That choice is not right. You have given the perineum a head's figure. A small patch is easy to match with the first nines you memorised.
Test it against the total: if the perineum took 9, the chart would pass 100%. Check the regions you know, then find the figure that fits.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the total before you commit: the adult chart sums to 100%.

say.text: That choice is not right. You have given the perineum a trunk-sized figure, as if it were a large region. Trunk figures are the big numbers, so they sound right.
The perineum is a small region, and the whole chart must still total 100%. Add the other regions, then choose the small figure.

sure_note.text: You were sure the perineum is a large region. It is small, and 18% would overshoot the total.

say.text: Yes. The perineum is 1%, which brings the adult chart to 100%.
For a small, patchy burn, the patient's palm including fingers is about 1% TBSA.
Count only partial and full thickness areas toward TBSA. Simple erythema is not counted.
A major burn needing formal resuscitation is generally over 15% in adults and over 10% in children.
